summary: The three-argument form of pow computes a modular power without constructing the full potentially huge integer power first.
documentation: The three-argument form of pow computes a modular power without constructing the full potentially huge integer power first. For nonnegative integer exponents and a positive modulus, the result is the remainder in the range zero through modulus minus one.
inputs: An object with integer base, nonnegative integer exponent and positive integer modulus, all small enough for exact JSON input.
caution: This arithmetic primitive alone is not a secure cryptographic protocol. The exercise excludes zero or negative moduli and negative exponents, whose rules differ.
scenarios: Compute a cyclic counter’s repeated multiplier under a fixed modulus.
Explore a small modular-arithmetic teaching example.
Verify bounded modular results in a local number-theory exercise.
title: Compute a modular power
problem: Return pow(base, exponent, modulus). Exponent is 0..100 and modulus is 1..1000. Base may be negative. Avoid constructing a giant intermediate power.
hint: Use all three arguments of pow.
goal: Use pow() with modulus or an equivalent approach demonstrating the same premise.
